title: Senior's toolkit: capacity and failure
summary: top, OOMKilled, node pressure, HPAs, PDBs and safe node drains.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: capacity and failure
steps.body: Reliability work is measuring real usage, reading why a container died, and taking nodes out without an outage.

toolkit.what: Live CPU and memory per container, from metrics-server. Compare it with requests and limits before you tune them.
flags: one line per container, not per pod

toolkit.what: Real CPU and memory use per node. A node near 100% memory starts evicting pods.
Why the last container instance died. `OOMKilled` means it went over its memory limit (exit code 137).
The `Allocated resources` table shows requests as a share of the node. Scheduling uses requests, not real use, so a node can be full while idle.
flags: sum of requests and limits on the node

toolkit.what: Watches the autoscaler: current against target utilisation and the replica count. `<unknown>` targets mean it has no metrics.
flags: events: why it did or did not scale

toolkit.what: PodDisruptionBudgets and how many disruptions each allows right now. `ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS 0` will block a drain.
Cordons a node and evicts its pods while respecting PDBs. The safe way to patch or replace a node.
flags: DaemonSet pods stay (they would come straight back)
allow evicting pods with `emptyDir` scratch data
give up instead of waiting forever

toolkit.what: Stop or allow new pods on a node without touching the running ones.

steps.prompt: The `api` pod shows `RESTARTS 14` and status flips between `Running` and `CrashLoopBackOff`. The logs end mid-request with no error. What do you check first?
options: `lastState.terminated.reason` (or `kubectl describe pod`) for `OOMKilled`, then `kubectl top pods --containers`
steps.explain: An app that dies with no error message was usually killed from outside. `OOMKilled` with exit code 137 means it went over its memory limit. Compare real use with the limit, then raise it or fix the leak.

steps.prompt: Match the output to what it means.
pairs: the container exceeded its memory limit
the pod's CPU request fits on no node
a drain will wait on these pods
the kubelet may start evicting pods

steps.prompt: Take a node out for patching, safely.
steps.explain: `drain` cordons and then evicts while honouring PDBs. `--force` and `--grace-period=0` skip the safety you want here.

steps.prompt: `kubectl drain` has printed `Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget` for five minutes. What do you do?
options: Check `kubectl get pdb -A`: the app needs more ready replicas (or a looser PDB) before one pod can leave
steps.explain: The drain is working as intended: removing that pod now would break the app's availability promise. Scale the app up or fix its unready pods; bypassing the PDB moves the outage onto the users.

steps.prompt: Which signal uses requests, and which uses real usage?
items: Whether a pod can be scheduled on a node

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Set requests from `kubectl top` numbers, not guesses, and check `lastState` before reading logs when a pod restarts. Before any node maintenance, look at `kubectl get pdb -A`, then `drain`: never delete pods by hand.
